'''William Oughtred'''  ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɔː|t|ə|r|d}} {{respelling|AWT|urd}};<ref>How to Pronounce: Oughtred Society [http://www.pronouncekiwi.com/Oughtred%20Society Retrieved 9 August 2018.]</ref><ref name="Smith19232">{{cite book |last1=Smith |first1=David Eugene |author-link=David Eugene Smith |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=12qdOZ0gsWoC&pg=PA392 |title=History of Mathematics |date=1923 |isbn=9780486204291 |volume=1 |page=392}}</ref>5 March 1574 – 30 June 1660),<ref name="Smith1923">{{cite book |first1=David Eugene |last1=Smith |author-link=David Eugene Smith |title=History of Mathematics |volume=1 |date=1923 |page=392 |publisher=Dover Publications |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=12qdOZ0gsWoC&pg=PA392|isbn=9780486204291 }}</ref> also '''Owtred''' or '''Uhtred''', was an English mathematician and [[Anglican clergyman]].<ref name=Bayle>'Oughtred (William)', in P. Bayle, translated and revised by J.P. Bernard, T. Birch and J. Lockman, ''A General Dictionary, Historical and Critical'', (James Bettenham, for G. Strachan and J. Clarke, London 1734/1739), Vol. VIII, [https://books.google.com/books?id=qGFZAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA77 pp. 77-86] (Google).</ref><ref>F. Willmoth, 'Oughtred, William (bap. 1575, d. 1660)', ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'' (2004).</ref><ref>{{Cite DNB|wstitle= Oughtred, William |last= Mullinger  |first= James Bass |author-link= James Bass Mullinger |volume=42 |pages=356-358 |short=1}}</ref> After [[John Napier]] discovered [[logarithm]]s and [[Edmund Gunter]] created the [[logarithmic scale]]s (lines, or rules) upon which [[slide rule]]s are based, Oughtred was the first known to use two such scales in separate rods sliding by one another to perform direct [[multiplication]] and [[division (mathematics)|division]]. He is credited with being second inventing the [[Slide rule scale|slide rule]] instrument in about 1632.<ref name="las_invenciones_de">{{Cite web |last=Fernández |first=Jose G. |date=20 July 2026 |title=Las Invenciones de Delamain y Oughtred |url=https://www.reglasdecalculo.com/presentaciones/DelamainyOughtred.html |url-status=live |access-date=31 August 2026 |website=www.reglasdecalculo.com}}</ref> He also introduced the "×" [[multiplication sign|symbol for multiplication]] and the abbreviations "sin" and "cos" for the [[sine and cosine]] functions.<ref>{{cite book |title=A History of Mathematics |author=Florian Cajori |year=1919 |publisher=Macmillan |url=https://archive.org/details/ahistorymathema02cajogoog|page=[https://archive.org/details/ahistorymathema02cajogoog/page/n169 157] |quote=cajori william-oughtred multiplication. |author-link=Florian Cajori }}</ref>

==Clerical life==
===Education===
The son of Benjamin Oughtred of [[Eton, Berkshire|Eton]] in [[Buckinghamshire]] (now part of [[Berkshire]]), William was born there on 5 March 1574/75 and was educated at [[Eton College]], where his father, a writing-master, was one of his teachers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wallis |first=P.J. |date=1968 |title=William Oughtred's 'Circles of Proportion' and 'Trigonometries' |journal=Transactions of the Cambridge Bibliographical Society |volume=4 |issue=5 |pages=372–382|jstor=41154471 }}</ref> Oughtred had a passion for mathematics, and often stayed awake at night to learn while others were sleeping.<ref name=":0">F. Cajori, ''William Oughtred, a Great Seventeenth-Century Teacher of Mathematics'' (Open Court Publishing Company, Chicago 1916), [https://archive.org/details/williamoughtredg00cajouoft/page/12/mode/2up?view=theater pp. 12-14] (Internet Archive).</ref> He next attended [[King's College, Cambridge]], where he graduated BA in 1596/97 and MA in 1600, holding a fellowship in the college from 1595 to 1603.<ref>{{acad |id=OTRT592W |name=Oughtred, William}}</ref> He composed a Funeral Ode in Latin for Sir [[William More (died 1600)|William More]] of [[Loseley Park]] in 1600.<ref>'Funeral ode by William Outhred', Surrey History Centre, [https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/8509617c-1cd9-4518-bcfa-dca78e3eb376 ref. 6729/7/129] (Discovery Catalogue).</ref>

===Rector at Guildford and at Shalford===
[[File:The Victoria history of the county of Surrey (1902) (20606618248).jpg|thumb|right|250px|The Caryll home at Great Tangley]]
Admitted to holy orders, he left the [[University of Cambridge]] about 1603, when as "Master" William Oughtred he held the rectorate of [[St Mary's Church, Guildford]], Surrey.<ref>Church of England Clergy database, Liber Cleri detail, [https://theclergydatabase.org.uk/jsp/DisplayLibClDetail.jsp?CDBLibClDeID=199392 CCEd Record ID: 199392], from British Library Harleian MS 595.</ref> At the presentation of the lay patron [[George Austen (MP)|George Austen]], gent., he was instituted as vicar at [[Shalford, Surrey|Shalford]] near [[Wonersh]], in the neighbourhood of [[Guildford]] in western [[Surrey]], on 2 July 1605.<ref>Church of England Clergy database, Episcopal Register of Thomas Bilson (Winchester), Appointment Record ("Owtred") [https://theclergydatabase.org.uk/jsp/DisplayAppointment.jsp?CDBAppRedID=59030 CCEd Record ID: 59030]. </ref>

On 20 February 1606, at Shalford, Oughtred married Christs-gift Caryll, a relation of the Caryll family seated at Great Tangley Hall at Shalford.<ref>''[[ODNB]]'', and see ''Aubrey's Brief Lives'', Ed. Oliver Lawson Dick (Ann Arbor, Michigan 1962), pp. 222–224.</ref><ref>'William Oughtred', in F. Willmoth, ''Sir Jonas Moore: Practical Mathematics and Restoration Science'' (The Boydell Press, Woodbridge 1993), pp. 43-61, [https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Sir_Jonas_Moore/Ku2IWu3xchoC?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PA45 at p. 45] (Google).</ref><ref>Christes-Guift Carell, daughter of William and Dorothy, was baptized at Godalming on 21 April 1588 (Register).</ref> The Oughtreds had twelve children, William,<ref>William Oughtred (Owtred) junr was baptized at Shalford on 9 October 1608 (Register): the younger children were baptized at Albury.</ref> Henry, Henry (the first Henry died as a baby), Benjamin, Simon, Margaret, Judith, Edward, Elizabeth, Anne, George, and John. Two of the sons, Benjamin and John, shared their father's interest in instruments and became watchmakers.<ref>J.J. O'Connor and E.F. Robertson, "Biographies: William Oughtred", MacTutor History of Mathematics archive, [https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Oughtred/ Last Update, 2017] (University of St Andrews).</ref>

Oughtred's wife was a cousin of Simon Caryll of Tangley and his wife Lady Elizabeth Aungier (married 1607), daughter of [[Francis Aungier, 1st Baron Aungier of Longford|Sir Francis Aungier]]. Oughtred was a witness to Simon Caryll's will, made 1618,<ref>London Metropolitan Archive ref. DW/PA/5/1619/22.</ref><ref>William "Owtred" also witnessed the first codicil (8 November 1620) to the Will of George Austen of Shalford (P.C.C. 1621, Dale quire).</ref> and through two further marriages Elizabeth remained matriarch and dowager of Great Tangley until her death in about 1650.<ref>W. Bruce Bannerman (ed.), ''The Visitations of the county of Surrey taken in the years 1530, 1572 and 1623'', Harleian Society Vol. XLIII (1899), [https://archive.org/stream/visitationsofcou43beno#page/88/mode/2up pp. 88–89] (Internet Archive).</ref><ref>Cf. Will of John Machell, Gentleman of Wonersh (P.C.C. 1647, Fine quire); Will of Elizabeth Machell of Wonersh (P.C.C. 1650, Pembroke quire).</ref> Elizabeth's brother Gerald, 2nd Baron Aungier of Longford, was married to Jane, daughter of Sir [[Edward Onslow (died 1615)|Edward Onslow]] of [[Cranleigh|Knowle, Surrey]], in 1638. Oughtred praised Gerald (whom he taught) as a man of great piety and learning, skilled in Latin, Greek, Hebrew and other oriental languages.<ref>E.W. Brayley, J. Britton and E.W Brayley jnr., ''A Topographical History of Surrey'' (G. Willis, London 1850), vol. II, [https://books.google.com/books?id=6PcGAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA49 p. 49] (Google). John Aubrey, ''The Natural History and Antiquities of the County of Surrey'', 5 vols (E. Curll, London 1718-19), III, [https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-natural-history-and-_aubrey-john_1718_3/page/258/mode/2up?view=theater at pp. 258-59] (Internet Archive), quotes Oughtred's original Latin for these remarks.</ref><ref>Gerald is sometimes referred to as "Gerard", but the name derives from his mother's family of Fitzgerald, seated at [[Hatchlands Park]] in [[East Clandon]].</ref>

In January 1610 Sir [[George More]], patron of [[Compton, Surrey|Compton]] church adjacent to [[Loseley Park]], granted the [[advowson]] (right of presentation of the minister) to Oughtred, when it should next fall vacant, though Oughtred was not thereby empowered to present himself to the living.<ref name=Yel /> This was soon after Sir George More became reconciled to the marriage of his daughter Anne to the poet [[John Donne]], which had occurred secretly in 1601.

===Rector of Albury===
Oughtred was presented by Sir Edward Randyll of [[Chilworth Manor, Surrey|Chilworth]] (lord of the manor) to the rectory of [[Albury, Surrey|Albury]], near [[Guildford]] in Surrey and instituted on 16 October 1610,<ref>Church of England Clergy database, Episcopal Register of Thomas Bilson (Winchester), Appointment Record, [https://theclergydatabase.org.uk/jsp/DisplayAppointment.jsp?CDBAppRedID=59103 CCEd Record ID: 59103]. The advowson was in the lord of the manor, who was Sir Edward.</ref> vacating Shalford on 18 January 1611.<ref>Church of England Clergy database, Episcopal Register of Thomas Bilson (Winchester), Vacancy Evidence Record ("Outhred"), [https://theclergydatabase.org.uk/jsp/DisplayVacancy.jsp?CDBAppRedID=59115 CCEd Record ID: 59115]</ref> 

In January 1615/16 Sir George More re-granted the advowson of Compton church (still occupied) in trust to Roger Heath and Simon Caryll, to present Oughtred himself, or any other person whom Oughtred should nominate, when the vacancy should arise.<ref>This was just one year after the ordination of John Donne (23 January 1615) and 6 months before his institution as rector of Sevenoaks (12 July 1616). The Clergy database, CCEd Ordination record [https://theclergydatabase.org.uk/jsp/DisplayOrdination.jsp?CDBOrdRedID=119823 ID 119823], and Appointment Evidence Record [https://theclergydatabase.org.uk/jsp/DisplayAppointment.jsp?CDBAppRedID=114560 ID 114560].</ref> Soon afterwards Oughtred was approached by John Tichborne seeking his own nomination, and entering an agreement to pay him a sum of money upon certain days. Before this could be completed the incumbent died (November 1618), and Oughtred sought for himself to be presented, preaching several times at Compton, having the [[Annates|first fruits]] sequestered to his use, and, after four months, asking the patron to present him. However, Tichborne offered to complete the agreed payment at once, and was accordingly presented by the trustees in May 1619 (Simon Caryll dying in that year): but before he could be admitted, the Crown interposed a different candidate because the contract between Oughtred and Tichborne was deemed by Sir [[Henry Yelverton (attorney-general)|Henry Yelverton]] clearly to be [[Simony|Simoniacal]].<ref name=Yel>"Yelverton, Sir Henry. Opinion that simony was involved in the contract between William Oughtred and John Tichborne for presentation to the church of Compton in Surrey", Papers of the More family of Loseley Park, Surrey, 1488-1682 (bulk 1538-1630), Surrey History Centre, [https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/42eaada0-9ac3-4f74-bd72-660a7992d99f ref. Z/407/Lb.668.4] (Discovery Catalogue). View original document at [https://digitalcollections.folger.edu/bib244741-309974-lb668 Folger Shakespeare Library]. See also "Interrogatories", S.H.C. [https://www.surreyarchives.org.uk/collections/getrecord/SHCOL_LM_SECTIONA_5_8_1_8 ref. LM/1329/104, 107, 109, 670] (Surrey History Centre Archives Catalogue).</ref>

[[File:Old St Peter and St Paul's Church, Albury Park, Albury (March 2014, from Southwest) (2).JPG|thumb|right|250px|[[Old St Peter and St Paul's Church, Albury]], Surrey, where William Oughtred was rector from 1610 to 1660, and where he is buried.]]
Oughtred therefore remained at Albury,<ref name="EB1911">{{Cite EB1911|wstitle=Oughtred, William|volume=20|page=378}}</ref> serving as [[rector (ecclesiastical)|rector]] there for fifty years.<ref>J. and J.A. Venn, ''Alumni Cantabrigienses'' Part 1 Vol. III (Cambridge University Press 1924), [https://archive.org/details/p1alumnicantabri03univuoft/page/288/mode/2up p. 288] (Internet Archive) (appointment 1610).</ref><ref>"Parishes: Albury", in H.E. Malden (ed.), ''A History of the County of Surrey'', Volume 3 (V.C.H./HMSO, London 1911), [https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/surrey/vol3/pp72-77#anchorn4 pp. 72-77] (British History Online): "was rector from 1610 to 1660".</ref> His patron, the [[Thomas Howard, 14th Earl of Arundel|Earl of Arundel]], acquired the fine old seat of Albury House through trustees in 1638: title to the manor was assigned in trust for payment of debts to George Duncombe (of Weston in Albury, embedded in the Carrill and Onslow interests), who maintained the manorial courts until his death in 1646, and then to Duncombe's children.<ref name=duncombe>'26 September 1651' and following, in M.A.E. Green (ed.), ''Calendar of the Proceedings of the Committee for Compounding, 1643-1660'', Part 4: Cases, July 1650 to December 1653 (HMSO 1892), [https://archive.org/details/cu31924024797890/page/2472/mode/2up?view=theater p. 2472] (Internet Archive). See also The National Archives (UK), Chancery, ''Duncumbe v Onslow'' (1651), [https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C5640690 ref. C 10/467/79] (Discovery Catalogue). </ref> The Park and landscapes,<ref>J. Aubrey, ''The Natural History and Antiquities of the County of Surrey'', 5 vols (E. Curll, London 1718-19), IV, [https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-natural-history-and-_aubrey-john_1718_4/page/n67/mode/2up?view=theater at pp. 65-70] (Internet Archive).</ref> which formed the subject of a series of etchings produced by [[Wenceslas Hollar]], c. 1645,<ref>The British Museum, Print Collections. Hollar: "Alburgum in Comitatu Surriæ, vulgo Albury", [https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/P_Q-6-89 ref. Q,6. 89] (The British Museum). See also a set of 6 Hollar views of Albury in Bonham's auction of Prints and Multiples, (2 May 2019, Knightsbridge, London) [https://www.bonhams.com/auction/25380/lot/7/wenceslaus-hollar-czech-1607-1677-views-of-countryside-near-albury-surrey-the-complete-set-of-six-etchings-c1645-on-laid-the-second-final-state-with-number-in-the-margin-each-88-x-156mm-3-12-x-6-18inpl6/ Lot 7] (Bonhams).</ref> were developed in this period, before a [[Committee for Compounding with Delinquents|parliamentary sequestration]] which was eventually discharged in 1653.<ref name=duncombe /> The Earl having died in 1646, and [[Henry Howard, 15th Earl of Arundel|his son and successor Henry]] (who renewed the assignment) in 1652, it was the grandson [[Henry Howard, 6th Duke of Norfolk|Henry Howard]] (later Duke of Norfolk) who finally paid for and acquired Albury.<ref>'Parishes: Albury', in H.E. Malden (ed.), ''A History of the County of Surrey'' Vol. 3 (VCH, London 1911), [https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/surrey/vol3/pp72-77 pp. 72-77, at fn 15 ff.] (British History Online).</ref>

[[William Lilly]], that celebrated astrologer, knew Oughtred and claimed in his autobiography to have intervened on his behalf to prevent his ejection from his living by Parliament in 1646:<blockquote>"About this time, the most famous mathematician of all Europe, Mr. William Oughtred, parson of Aldbury in Surry, was in danger of [[sequestration (law)|sequestration]] by the [[Committee for Plundered Ministers|Committee of or for plundered ministers]]; ([[wiktionary:ambodexter|Ambo-dexters]] they were;)<ref>"Ambo-dexters", in the figurative meaning, i.e. their allegiances swayed according to their own advantage.</ref> several inconsiderable articles were deposed and sworn against him, material enough to have sequestered him, but that, upon his day of hearing, I applied myself to Sir [[Bulstrode Whitelocke|Bolstrode Whitlock]], and all my own old friends, who in such numbers appeared in his behalf, that though the chairman and many other Presbyterian members were stiff against him, yet he was cleared by the major number."<ref name=Lilly>''William Lilly's History of his Life and Times, from the year 1602 to 1681'' (Published London 1715), Reprint (Charles Baldwyn, London 1822), [https://archive.org/details/williamlillyshi00ashmgoog/page/n164 pp. 135-37] (Internet Archive).</ref></blockquote> Of his portrait (aged 73, 1646) engraved by Wenceslas Hollar, prefixed to the ''Clavis Mathematica'', [[John Evelyn]] remarked that it "extreamly resembles him", and that it showed "that calm and placid Composure, which seemed to proceed from, and be the result of some happy ''ἕυρησις'' and Invention".<ref>J. Evelyn, ''Numismata: A Disccourse of Medals, Ancient and Modern... To which is added, A Discourse concerning Physiognomy'' (Benjamin Tooke, London 1697), [https://books.google.com/books?id=hpJMAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA341 p. 341] (Google).</ref> William Oughtred died at Albury in 1660, a month after the restoration of [[Charles II of England|Charles II]]. A staunch supporter of the royalty, he is said to have died of joy at the knowledge of the return of the King. He was buried in [[Old St Peter and St Paul's Church, Albury]].<ref>"Parishes: Albury", in H.E. Malden (ed.), ''A History of the County of Surrey'', Volume 3 (V.C.H./HMSO, London 1911), [http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/surrey/vol3/pp72-77 pp. 72-77] (British History Online, accessed 6 December 2018).</ref> Autobiographical information is contained in his address "To the English gentrie" in his ''Just Apologie'' of c. 1634.<ref>(W. Oughtred), ''To the English gentrie, and all others studious of the mathematicks which shall bee readers hereof. The just apologie of Wil: Oughtred, against the slaunderous insimulations of Richard Delamain, in a pamphlet called Grammelogia, or the Mathematicall Ring, or Mirifica Logarithmorum Projectio Circularis'' (A. Mathewes, London ?1634). Full text at [https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo2/A08589.0001.001?view=toc Umich/eebo]. Extracts in F. Cajori (1915) (Further reading).</ref>

==Mathematician==
Oughtred developed his interest in mathematics early in life, and devoted whatever spare time his academic studies allowed him to it. Among the short tracts added to the 1647/48 editions of the ''Clavis Mathematica'' was one describing a natural and easy way of delineating sun-dials upon any surface, however positioned, which the author states he invented in his 23rd year (1597/98), which is to say, during his fellowship at [[King's College, Cambridge]]. His early preoccupation was to find a portable instrument or dial by which to find the hour, he tried various contrivances, but never to his satisfaction. "At last, considering that all manner of questions concerning the first motions were performed most properly by the Globe itself, rectified to the present elevation  by the help of a moveable [[Azimuth]]; he projected the Globe upon the plane of the Horizon, and applied to it at the center, which was therein the [[Zenith]], an Index with projected degrees, for the moveable Azimuth."<ref name=Bayle /> 

[[File:Oughtred's circular slide rule with sundial on reverse, Elias Allen, London, c. 1633-1640 - Putnam Gallery - Harvard University - DSC07908.jpg|thumb|left|250px|An instrument for Oughtred's "Circles of Proportion", by Elias Allen, c. 1633–1640 (Harvard University, Putnam Gallery)]]
This projection answered his search, but then he had to invent theorems, problems and methods to calculate sections and intersections of large circles, which he could not find by instruments, not having access to any of sufficient size. In this way he drew out his findings, presenting one example to Bishop [[Thomas Bilson]] (who had ordained him), and another, in about 1606, to a certain noble lady, for whom he wrote notes for its use. In London, in spring 1618, Oughtred visited his friend [[Henry Briggs (mathematician)|Henry Briggs]] at [[Gresham College]], and was introduced to [[Edmund Gunter]], Reader in Astronomy, then occupying Dr Brooks's rooms. He showed Gunter his "Horizontall Instrument", who questioned him closely about it and spoke very approvingly. Soon afterwards Gunter sent him a print taken from a brass instrument made by [[Elias Allen]], after Oughtred's written instructions (which Allen preserved).<ref name=Bayle /> When, in 1632, [[Richard Delamain]] the elder claimed that invention for himself,<ref>M. Selinger, ''Teaching Mathematics'' (1994), p. 142.</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://galileo.rice.edu/Catalog/NewFiles/delamain.html |title=The Galileo Project |publisher=Galileo.rice.edu |access-date=31 October 2012}}</ref> William Robinson wrote to Oughtred: "I cannot but wonder at the indiscretion of Rich. Delamain, who being conscious to himself that he is but the pickpurse of another man's wit, would thus inconsiderately provoke and awake a sleeping lion..."<ref>'VII: W. Robinson to Oughtred', in S.J. Rigaud (ed.), ''Correspondence of Scientific Men of the Seventeenth Century'', 2 vols (University Press, Oxford 1841), I [https://books.google.com/books?id=oBnP1vRoAOcC&pg=PA11 pp. 11-14] (Google).</ref>

Around 1628 he was appointed by the [[Thomas Howard, 21st Earl of Arundel|Earl of Arundel]] to instruct his son William Howard in mathematics.<ref name="EB1911"/> Some of Oughtred's mathematical correspondence survives, and is printed in [[Pierre Bayle|Bayle]]'s ''General Dictionary'',<ref name=Bayle /> and (with some editorial omissions restored) in [[Stephen Peter Rigaud|Rigaud]]'s ''Correspondence of Scientific Men''.<ref>Letters II-XXXVI, in S.P. Rigaud and S.J. Rigaud (eds), ''Correspondence of Scientific Men of the Seventeenth Century'', 2 vols (University Press, Oxford 1841), I, [https://books.google.com/books?id=oBnP1vRoAOcC&pg=PA3 pp. 3-92] (Google).</ref> [[William Alabaster]] wrote to him in 1633 to propose the quadrature of the circle by consideration of the fourth chapter of the [[Book of Ezekiel]].<ref>Bayle, ''General Dictionary'', VIII, [https://books.google.com/books?id=qGFZAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA80 p. 80, note, col. b] (Google).</ref> In 1634 he corresponded with the French architect [[François Derand]], and (among others) with [[Sir Charles Cavendish]] (1635), [[Johannes Banfi Hunyades]] (1637), [[William Gascoigne (scientist)|William Gascoigne]] (1640)<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.dspace.cam.ac.uk/handle/1810/194216|hdl=1810/194216 |journal=DSpace at Cambridge|title= Letter from William Gascoigne to William Oughtred |publisher=University of Cambridge |date=13 June 2007 |access-date=31 October 2012}}</ref> and Dr John Twysden, M.D. (1650).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://janus.lib.cam.ac.uk/db/node.xsp?id=CV%2FPers%2FOughtred%2C%20William%20(%3F%201574-1660)%20mathematician |title=Janus: Oughtred, William (? 1574-1660) mathematician |publisher=Janus.lib.cam.ac.uk |access-date=31 October 2012 |archive-date=29 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230729205528/https://janus.lib.cam.ac.uk/db/node.xsp?id=CV%2FPers%2FOughtred%2C%20William%20%28%3F%201574-1660%29%20mathematician |url-status=dead }}</ref> 

Oughtred offered free mathematical tuition to pupils, among them [[William Forster (mathematician)|William Forster]] and [[Jonas Moore]], and his teaching influenced a generation of mathematicians. [[Seth Ward (bishop)|Seth Ward]] resided with Oughtred for six months to learn contemporary mathematics, and the physician [[Charles Scarborough]] also stayed at Albury: [[John Wallis]] and [[Christopher Wren]] corresponded with him.<ref>[[Helena Pycior|H.M. Pycior]], ''Symbols, Impossible Numbers, and Geometric Entanglements: British Algebra Through the Commentaries on Newton's Universal Arithmetick'' (1997), p. 42.</ref> Another Albury pupil was [[Robert Wood (mathematician)|Robert Wood]], who helped him to see the ''Clavis'' through the press.<ref>T.C. Barnard, ''Cromwellian Ireland: English Government and Reform in Ireland 1649–1660'' (2000), p. 223.</ref> [[Isaac Newton]]'s high opinion of Oughtred is expressed in his letter of 1694 to Nathaniel Hawes, where he quotes him extensively, calling him "a Man whose judgement (if any man's) may safely be relyed upon... that very good and judicious man, Mr Oughtred".<ref>'Appendix. No. XXV. Newton to Hawes', in J. Edleston (ed.), ''Correspondence of Sir Isaac Newton and Professor Cotes, Including Letters of Other Eminent Men'' (John W. Parker, London/John Deighton, Cambridge 1850), pp. 279-92, [https://books.google.com/books?id=jQI-9EMUloQC&pg=PA291 at pp. 291-92] (Google).</ref>

The first edition of John Wallis's foundational text on [[infinitesimal calculus]], ''Arithmetica Infinitorum'' (1656), carries a long letter of dedication to William Oughtred.<ref>J. Wallis, ''Arithmetica Infinitorum, sive Nova Methodus Inquirendi in Curvisineorum Quadraturam'' (Typis Leon: Lichfield Academiae Typographi, Impensis Tho. Robinson, Oxford 1656), [https://archive.org/details/ArithmeticaInfinitorum/page/n7/mode/2up?view=theater unpaginated front matter] (Internet Archive).</ref>

==Publications==

===''Clavis Mathematicæ'' (1631)===
[[File:Vandyck - willianhoward01.jpg|thumb|left|200px|William Howard]]
William Oughtred's most important work was first published in 1631, in Latin, under the title ''Arithemeticæ in Numeris et Speciebus Institutio, quae tum Logisticæ, tum Analyticæ, atque adeus totius Mathematicæ quasi Clavis est'' (i.e. "The Foundation of Arithmetic in Numbers and Kinds, which is as it were the Key of the Logistic, then of the Analytic, and so of the whole Mathematic(s)"). It was dedicated to [[William Howard, 1st Viscount Stafford|William Howard]], youngest son of Oughtred's patron [[Thomas Howard, 14th Earl of Arundel]].<ref>(Londini, apud Thomam Harperum, 1631): see full page-views at [https://books.google.com/books?id=7kImAAAAcAAJ Google].</ref> 

[[File:Oughtred - Clavis mathematicae, 1652 - BEIC 4625537.tiff|thumb|''Clavis mathematicae'', 1652 edition]]
This is a textbook on elementary algebra. It begins with a discussion of the Hindu-Arabic notation of decimal fractions and later introduces multiplication and division sign abbreviations of decimal fractions. Oughtred also discussed two ways to perform long division and introduced the "~" symbol, in terms of mathematics, expressing the difference between two variables. ''Clavis Mathematicae'' became a classic, reprinted in several editions. It was used as a textbook by [[John Wallis]] and [[Isaac Newton]] among others.  A concise work, it argued for a less verbose style in mathematics, and greater dependence on symbols. Drawing on [[François Viète]] (though not explicitly), Oughtred also innovated freely with symbols, introducing not only the multiplication sign as now used universally,<ref>F. Cajori, 'The cross X as a symbol for multiplication', ''Nature'', Vol. XCIV (1914), Abstract, [https://www.nature.com/articles/094363c0 pp. 363-64] (journal's webpage).</ref> but also the [[proportion sign]] (double colon ::).<ref>[[Helena Pycior|Helena Mary Pycior]], ''Symbols, Impossible Numbers, and Geometric Entanglements: British Algebra Through the Commentaries on Newton's Universal Arithmetick'' (1997), p. 48.</ref> The first edition, 1631, contained 20 chapters and 88 pages including algebra and various fundamentals of mathematics.<ref>{{Cite journal |journal= The Monist|volume= 25|issue= 3|pages= 441–466|language=en |jstor = 27900548|last1 = Cajori|first1 = Florian|title= The Works of William Oughtred|year= 1915|doi= 10.5840/monist191525315|url= https://zenodo.org/record/1514882}}</ref> 

The work was recast for the ''New'' Key, which appeared first in an English edition of 1647, ''The Key of the Mathematicks New Forged and Filed'', dedicated to Sir [[Richard Onslow (Parliamentarian)|Richard Onslow]] and to his son [[Sir Arthur Onslow, 1st Baronet|Arthur Onslow]] (son and grandson of Sir Edward), and then in a Latin edition of 1648, entitled ''Clavis Mathematica Denuo Limata, sive potius Fabricata'' (i.e. "The Mathematical Key Newly Filed, or rather Made"), in which the preface was removed and the book was reduced by one chapter. In the English Foreword, Oughtred explains that the intention had always been to provide the ingenious reader with an ''[[Ariadne's thread (logic)|Ariadne's thread]]'' through the intricate labyrinth of these studies, but that his earlier, highly compressed style had been found difficult by some, and was now further elucidated.<ref>Bayle, 'Oughtred (William)', ''General Dictionary'', VIII, [https://books.google.com/books?id=qGFZAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA78 p. 78, note col. a] (Google).</ref> These editions contained additional tracts on the resolution of adfected equations proposed in numbers, and other materials necessary for the use of decimal parts and logarithms, as well as his work on delineating sundials.<ref>G.''[W.]'' Oughtred, ''Clavis Mathematica Denuo Limata, sive potius Fabricata'' (Londini, Excudebat Thomas Harper, sumptibus Thome Whitakeri, apud quem venales sunt in Cœmiterio D. Pauli, 1648); Full page views at [https://books.google.com/books?id=ddMxgr27tNkC Google].</ref>

The last lifetime edition (third) was in 1652, and posthumous editions (as ''Clavis Mathematicæ'': i.e. "The Key of Mathematic(s)") appeared in 1667 and 1693 (Latin), and in 1694 (English). The work gained popularity around 15 years after it first appeared, as mathematics took a greater role in higher education. Wallis wrote the introduction to his 1652 edition, and used it to publicise his skill as [[cryptographer]];<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/about/oxford-figures/ch1-6a |title=Oxford Figures, Chapter 1: 800 years of mathematical traditions|publisher= Mathematical Institute – University of Oxford |date=17 September 2007 |access-date=31 October 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121026050151/http://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/about/oxford-figures/ch1-6a |archive-date=26 October 2012 }}</ref> in another, Oughtred promoted the talents of Wren.

===''The Circles of Proportion and the Horizontal Instrument'' (1632)===
[[File:Wenceslas Hollar - Arundel House, from the N..jpg|thumb|right|320px|]]
[[File:Wenceslas Hollar - Arundel House, from the S..jpg|thumb|right|320px|Arundel House, (above), looking south; (below), looking north.<ref name=versus>The captions "Versus Septentrionem", "versus Meridiem", suggest the opposite orientation, but the river Thames (to the south) is clearly visible in the "Septentrio" scene.</ref> By Adam Bierling with Wenceslas Hollar, 1646.]]
This work<ref>W. Oughtred, ed. W. Forster, ''The Circles of Proportion and the Horizontall Instrument. The former shewing the maner how to work proportions both simple and compound: and the ready and easy resolving of quæstions both in arithmetic, geometrie, & astronomie: and is newly increased with an additament for navigation. All which rules may also be wrought with the penne by arithmetic, and the canon of triangles. The latter teaching how to work most quæstions, which may be performed by the globe: and to delineat dialls upon any kind of plaine. Both invented, and the uses of both written in Latine by Mr. W. O. Translated into English and set forth for the publique benefit by William Forster'' First issue (Printed for Elias Allen maker of these and all other Mathematical Instruments and are to be sold at his shop over against St Clements church without Temple Bar, London 1632); Second issue (Printed by Augustine Mathewes, and are to bee sold by Nic: Bourne at the Royall Exchange, London 1633), full text at [https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo2/A08582.0001.001/1:2?rgn=div1;view=toc Umich/eebo].</ref> was based in many Oughtred notes before it was translated, compiled and edited for publication by his pupil, [[William Forster (mathematician)|William Forster]].<ref>{{cite DNB |wstitle=Forster, William (fl.1632) |volume=20}}</ref> Here Oughtred introduced the abbreviations for [[trigonometric functions]]. It contains his description and instructions for the use of his Horizontal Instrument and his Circles of Proportion, a [[slide rule]] disc with two cursors, that he invented with the assistance of [[Elias Allen]] (master instrument maker), being the second in inventing a [[slide rule]], after the separate invention of [[Richard Delamaine|Richard Delamain]] of two rings each with a logarithmic scale and no cursor.<ref name="las_invenciones_de" />

Oughtred with his student, William Forster, and Richard Delamain the elder, are concerned with the story of this book.<ref>A.J. Turner, 'William Oughtred, Richard Delamain and the Horizontal Instrument in seventeenth-century England', ''Annali dell'Istituto e Museo di storia della scienza di Firenze'' vol. 6 pt. 2 (1981), pp. 99-125.</ref>  As instructor to the Earl of Arundel's son, Oughtred had the use of a room in [[Arundel House]], the Earl's residence in the [[Strand, London|Strand]], in London. It is not clear how much instruction he gave there to Richard Delamain (who had already learned mathematics from [[Edmund Gunter]] lectures and chats at his rooms in Gresham College), and whom he found to be too dependent on mathematical instruments (like Gunter) to get a proper grasp of the theory behind them. On the other hand, his student William Forster, who came to him as a beginner during the 1620s, was fully taught without reference to instruments so that he should have a true grounding.<ref name=justapol>(W. Oughtred), ''To the English gentrie, and all others studious of the mathematicks which shall bee readers hereof. The Just Apologie of Wil: Oughtred, against the slaunderous insimulations of Richard Delamain, in a pamphlet called Grammelogia, or The Mathematicall Ring, or Mirifica Logarithmorum Projectio Circularis'' (A. Mathewes, London ?1634). Full text at [https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo2/A08589.0001.001?view=toc Umich/eebo].</ref> However, during the long vacation of 1630 Forster (who taught mathematics from a house in [[St Clement Danes]] churchyard, on the Westminster side of [[Temple Bar, London|Temple Bar]], in the same locality as [[Elias Allen]]'s shop), while staying with Oughtred at Albury, asked him about Gunter's Ruler, and was shown two hand prototypes done by his master, including Oughtred's circular slide rule prototype (for him, by then, only a toy).<ref name=Epistle>"To the Honourable and Renowned for vertue, learning, and true valour, Sir Kenelme Digbye, Knight (dated 1632)", in W. Oughtred, ed. W. Forster, ''The Circles of Proportion and the Horizontall Instrvment'' (1632, second issue 1633), [https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo2/A08582.0001.001/1:2?rgn=div1;view=fulltext unpaginated front matter]; also [https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo2/A08582.0001.001/1:3?rgn=div1;view=fulltext here] (Umich/eebo).</ref>

[[File:Wenceslas Hollar - Elias Allen.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Elias Allen, by Hollar: Oughtred's instrument-maker]]
Oughtred then said to Forster:<blockquote>"... the true way of Art is not by Instruments, but by Demonstration: and ... it is a preposterous course of vulgar Teachers, to begin with Instruments, and not with the Sciences, and so in-stead of Artists, to make their Schollers only doers of tricks, and as it were Iuglers: to the despite of Art, losse of precious time, and betraying of willing and industrious wits, unto ignorance, and idlenesse. ... the use of Instruments is indeed excellent, if a man be an Artist: but contemptible, being set and opposed to Art. And lastly, ... he meant to commend to me, the skill of Instruments, but first he would have me well instructed in the Sciences."<ref name=Epistle /></blockquote>

Forster, as Oughtred did not want to be involved with such devices, obtained Oughtred's permission to translate, edit and publish the many notes with the descriptions, explanations and instructions which Oughtred had of the Circles of Proportion and of the Horizontal Instrument (device to be used in Astronomy calculations), finishing his work in 1632.<ref name=Epistle /> However, for the final development of the Circles of Proportion as an instrument, he accepted the indications from Elias Allen to integrate an index of two arms instead of the "ring and a thread" from his prototype<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ougthred |first=William |title=The just Apology of Wil. Oughtred, against the slanderous accusations of Richard Delamain, in a Pamphlet called Grammelogia, or the Mathematical Ring, or Mirifica logarithmorum projection circularis.}}</ref>. Previously, Delamain had been writing-up his own description and account of a different instrument and having it manufactured. Delamain came off the press first, with a real instrument made by [[Elias Allen]], being then the inventor of the slide rule, and dedicating the treatise to King [[Charles I of England|Charles I]] to whom he gave the instrument and from who he obtained a patent. In his publication preamble, Forster, who dedicated ''The Circles of Proportion'' to the famous intellectual Sir [[Kenelm Digby]], commented that another person had hastily anticipated Oughtred's publication, with other hard comments on Delamain, thus beginning a strong argument.<ref name=Epistle /> After Delamain response in his Grammelogia second edition, it was left to Oughtred himself to publish his ''Just Apologie'' explaining his opinion on the priority of his inventions and writings, and arguing the behaviour of Delamain.<ref name=justapol /><ref>F.J. Swetz, 'Mathematical Treasure: Oughtred's Defense of His Slide Rule', ''Convergence'' (Online Periodical of the Mathematical Association of America), [https://www.maa.org/press/periodicals/convergence/mathematical-treasure-oughtreds-defense-of-his-slide-rule August 2018] (MAA).</ref><ref>For a recent account more sympathetic to Delamaine, see V. Keller, ''The Interlopers: Early Stuart Projects and the Undisciplining of Knowledge'' (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2023), [https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/The_Interlopers/92-ZEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PA230 at pp. 230-32] (Google).</ref>

===''Trigonometria'', with ''Canones Sinuum'' (1657)===
''Trigonometria, Hoc est, Modus Computandi Triangulorum Latera & Angulos'' was a collection compiled from Oughtred's papers by Richard Stokes and Arthur Haughton.<ref>W. Oughtred, ed. R. Stokes and A. Haughton, ''Trigonometria, Hoc est, Modus Computandi Triangulorum Latera & Angulos Ex Canone Mathematico traditus et demonstratus... Una cum Tabulis Sinuum, Tangent & Secant, &c.'' (Londini, Typis R. & L.W. Leybourn, Impensis Thomæ Johnson, apud quem væneunt sub signo Clavis Aureæ in Cœmiterio S. Pauli, 1657); full page views at [https://archive.org/details/trigonometria00ough/page/n5/mode/2up?view=theater Internet Archive].</ref> It contains about 36 pages of writing. Here the abbreviations for the [[trigonometric functions]] are explained in further detail consisting of mathematical tables.<ref name=":0" /> It carries a frontispiece portrait of Oughtred similar to that by Wenceslas Hollar, but re-engraved by [[William Faithorne]], and depicted as aged 83, and with a short epigram by "R.S." beneath. Longer verses addressed to Oughtred are prefixed by [[Christopher Wase]].

===''Opuscula Mathematica'' (1677)===
A miscellaneous collection of his hitherto unpublished mathematical papers (in Latin) was edited and published by his friend Sir [[Charles Scarborough]] in 1677.<ref>'William Oughtred', in O. Manning and Bray, ''The History and Antiquities of the County of Surrey'' (John White/John Nichols and Son, London 1804-14), II, [https://books.google.com/books?id=Yms-AQAAIAAJ&pg=PA132 pp. 132-33] (Google).</ref><ref>W. Oughtred, ed. C. Scarborough, ''Gulielmi Oughtredi Ætonensis, quondam Collegii Regalis Cantabrigia Socii, Opuscula Mathematica hactenus inedita'' (E Theatro Sheldoniano, Oxford 1677); Full pageviews at [https://books.google.com/books?id=WWcVAAAAQAAJ Google].</ref> The treatises contained are on these subjects:
[[File:William Oughtred plaque.jpg|thumb|right|250px|Plaque in the [[Old St Peter and St Paul's Church, Albury]]]]
* Institutiones Mechanicæ.
* De variis corporum generibus gravitate et magnitudine comparatis.
* Automata
* Quæstiones Diophanti Alexandrini Lib. 3
* De Triangulis planis rectangulis
* De Divisione Superficierum
* Musicæ Elementa
* De Propugnaculorum Munitionibus
* Sectiones Angulares

==Inventions==
===Slide rule===
Oughtred's invention of the slide rule consisted of taking a single "rule", already known to Gunter, and simplifying the method of employing it. Gunter required the use of a [[pair of dividers]] to lay off distances on his rule; Oughtred made the step of sliding two rules past each other to achieve the same ends.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hpmuseum.org/sliderul.htm |title=Slide Rules |publisher=Hpmuseum.org |access-date=31 October 2012}}</ref> His original design of some time in the 1620s was for a [[circular slide rule]]; but he was not the first into print with this idea, which was published by Delamain in 1630. The conventional design of a sliding middle section for a linear rule was an invention of the 1650s.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.powerhousemuseum.com/collection/database/theme,805,The_slide_rule_-_a_forgotten_tool |title=The slide rule – a forgotten tool |publisher=Powerhouse Museum Collection |access-date=31 October 2012}}</ref>

===Double horizontal sun dial===
At the age of 23, Oughtred invented the [[double horizontal sundial]], now named the Oughtred type after him.<ref>{{cite web
|url=http://dssmhi1.fas.harvard.edu/emuseumdev/code/emuseum.asp?collection=35&collectionname=PUTNAM%20GALLERY&style=browse&currentrecord=49&page=collection&profile=objects&searchdesc=PUTNAM%20GALLERY&sessionid=6B90C135-F283-4B64-A4B0-44A78572B173&action=collection&style=single&currentrecord=54 |title=Harvard University – Department of History of Science |publisher=Dssmhi1.fas.harvard.edu |access-date=31 October 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120220013142/http://dssmhi1.fas.harvard.edu/emuseumdev/code/emuseum.asp?collection=35&collectionname=PUTNAM%20GALLERY&style=browse&currentrecord=49&page=collection&profile=objects&searchdesc=PUTNAM%20GALLERY&sessionid=6B90C135-F283-4B64-A4B0-44A78572B173&action=collection&style=single&currentrecord=54 |archive-date=20 February 2012}}</ref> A short description ''The description and use of the double Horizontall Dyall'' (16 pp.) was added to a 1653 edition (in English translation) of the pioneer book on [[recreational mathematics]], ''Récréations Mathématiques'' (1624) by Hendrik van Etten, a pseudonym of [[Jean Leurechon]].<ref>W. Oughtred, 'The Description, and use of the double Horizontall Diall', in H. van Etten, ''Mathematicall recreations. Or, A collection of many problemes, extracted out of the ancient and modern philosophers'' (William Leake, London 1653), [https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo/A48262.0001.001/1:143?rgn=div1;view=fulltext unnumbered pages], full text at Umich/eebo.</ref> The translation itself is no longer attributed to Oughtred, but (probably) to Francis Malthus.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://logica.ugent.be/albrecht/thesis/Etten-intro.pdf |title=Récréations Mathématiques (1624) A Study on its Authorship, Sources and Influence |last=Heefer |first=Albrecht |website=logica.ugent.be }}</ref>

===Universal equinoctial ring dial===
Oughtred also invented the [[Sundial#Universal_equinoctial_ring_dial|Universal equinoctial ring dial]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://collections.rmg.co.uk/collections/objects/10369.html |title=Royal Museums Greenwich}}</ref>

==Occult interests==
According to his contemporaries, Oughtred had interests in [[alchemy]] and [[astrology]].<ref>[[Keith Thomas (historian)|Keith Thomas]], ''Religion and the Decline of Magic'' (1973), p. 322 and 452n.</ref> The [[Hermeticism|Hermetic science]] remained a philosophical touchstone among many reputable scientists of his time, and his student [[Thomas Henshaw (alchemist)|Thomas Henshaw]] copied a Diary and "Practike" given to him by his teacher.<ref>D.R. Dickson, 'Thomas Henshaw and Sir Robert Paston's pursuit of the Red Elixir: an early collaboration between Fellows of the Royal Society', ''Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London'', Vol. 51, No. 1 (Jan. 1997), pp. 57-76, at pp. 67-72.</ref> He was well-acquainted with the astrologer [[William Lilly]] who, as noted above, helped to prevent his ejection from his living in 1646.

===John Aubrey: Astrology and Geomancy===
[[John Aubrey]] states that (despite their political differences) [[Richard Onslow (Parliamentarian)|Sir Richard Onslow]], son of Sir Edward, also defended Oughtred against ejection in 1646. He adds that Oughtred was an astrologer, and successful in the use of [[natal astrology]], and used to say that he did not know why it should be effective, but believed that some "genius" or "spirit" assisted. According to Aubrey, [[Elias Ashmole]] possessed the original copy in Oughtred's handwriting of his rational division of the twelve houses of the [[zodiac]]. Oughtred penned an approving testimonial, dated 16 October 1659, to the foot of the English abstract of ''The Cabal of the Twelve Houses Astrological'' by "Morinus" ([[Jean-Baptiste Morin (mathematician)|Jean-Baptiste Morin]]) which [[Sir George Wharton, 1st Baronet|George Wharton]] inserted in his [[Almanac]] for 1659.<ref>'The Cabal of the Twelve Houses Astrological', collected in J. Gadbury (ed.), ''The Works of that Late Most Excellent Philosopher and Astronomer, Sir George Wharton, bar. collected into one volume'' (M.H. for John Leigh, London 1683), pp. 189-208, [https://books.google.com/books?id=LBroWVBBY2oC&pg=pa208 at p. 208] (Google).</ref>

[[File:Elias Ashmole.jpg|thumb|right|250px|Portrait bust of Elias Ashmole, 1656, by William Faithorne]]
Aubrey suggests that Oughtred was happy to allow the country people to believe that he was capable of conjuring. Aubrey himself had seen a copy of [[Christopher Cattan]]'s work on [[Geomancy]]<ref>''La Geomance du Seigneur Christofe de Cattan, Gentilhomme Genevoys. Livre non moins plaisant et recreatif. Avec la roüe de Pythagoras'' (Gilles Gilles, Paris 1558). Full text (page views) at [https://archive.org/details/lageomancedvseig00catt/page/n3 Internet Archive].</ref> annotated by Oughtred.<ref>Oughtred may have possessed the English translation by Francis Sparry, ''The Geomancie of Maister Christopher Catton, a Booke no lesse pleasant and recreative, then of a wittie invention'' (London 1591).</ref> He reported that Oughtred had told [[Seth Ward (bishop of Salisbury)|Bishop Ward]] and Elias Ashmole that he had received sudden intuitions or solutions to problems when standing in particular places, or leaning against a particular oak or ash tree, "as if infused by a divine genius", after having pondered those problems unsuccessfully for months or years.<ref>'William Oughtred, 1575-1660', in R. Barber (ed.), ''John Aubrey - Brief Lives: A selection based upon existing contemporary portraits'' (Folio Society, London 1975), 232-37.</ref>

===Elias Ashmole: Freemasonry===
Oughtred was well-known to [[Elias Ashmole]], as Ashmole stated in a note to Lilly's autobiographical sketch: "This gentleman I was very well acquainted with, having lived at the house over-against his, at Aldbury in Surrey, three or four years. E.A."<ref name=Lilly /> 

The biography of Ashmole in the ''[[Biographia Britannica]]'' (1747)<ref>W. Oldys (ed.), ''Biographia Britannica: or, the Lives of the most eminent persons who have flourished in Great Britain and Ireland'', 6 vols (W. Innys (etc.), London 1747-1766), I, pp. 223-36, [https://books.google.com/books?id=OIlDAAAAcAAJ&pg=pa224 at p. 224, note E, 'Collections relating to the history of Free-Masons'], and [https://books.google.com/books?id=OIlDAAAAcAAJ&pg=pa229 pp. 228-29] (Google).</ref> called forth the supposition that Oughtred was a participant in Ashmole's admission to [[freemasonry]] in 1646. [[Christoph Friedrich Nicolai|Friedrich Nicolai]], in both sections of his Essay (on the Templar and Masonic Orders) of 1783, associated Oughtred, Lilly, Wharton and other Astrologers in the formation of the order of Free and Accepted Masons in [[Warrington]] and London.<ref>C.F. Nicolai, ''Versuch über die Beschuldigungen welche dem Tempelherrenorden gemacht worden, und über dessen Geheimniß: Nebst einem Anhange über das Entstehen der Freymaurergesellschaft'' (Nicolai, Berlin und Stettin 1782), Theil I, [https://books.google.com/books?id=Lw8MAAAAYAAJ&pg=pa188 at p. 188]; Theil II, [https://books.google.com/books?id=0rtAAAAAcAAJ&pg=pa191 pp. 191-196] (Google).</ref> The statement was reinforced through repetition by [[Thomas De Quincey]],<ref>T. De Quincey, 'Historico-Critical Inquiry into the Origins of the Rosicrucians and the Free-Masons', in D. Masson (ed.), ''The Collected Writings of Thomas De Quincey'', New and Enlarged Edition, Vol. XIII: Tales and Prose Phantasies (Adam and Charles Black, Edinburgh 1890), [https://books.google.com/books?id=uhaaAAAAIAAJ&pg=pa425 at pp. 425-26] (Google).</ref> and elaborated by [[Jean-Marie Ragon]],<ref>J.M. Ragon, ''Orthodoxie maçonnique: suivie de la Maçonnerie occulte et de l'initiation hermétique'' (E. Dentu, Paris 1853), [https://books.google.com/books?id=fyF-4D4kAzsC&pg=PA28 pp. 28-33], [https://books.google.com/books?id=fyF-4D4kAzsC&pg=PA99 pp. 99-108], and ''passim'' (Google).</ref> but was debunked in [[Albert Gallatin Mackey|A.G. Mackey]]'s ''History of Freemasonry'' (1906).<ref>A.G. Mackey, ''The History of Freemasonry'', 2 volumes (The Masonic History Company, New York and London 1906), II, [https://archive.org/details/MackeyAGTheHistoryOfFreemasonryVol.II1906/page/n51/mode/2up?view=theater pp. 306, 316-18] (Internet Archive).</ref> 

Ashmole noted that he paid a visit to "Mr. Oughtred, the famous mathematician", on 15 September 1654, about three weeks after the Astrologers' Feast of that year.<ref>'The Life of Elias Ashmole, Esq.', in ''The Lives of Those Eminent Antiquaries Elias Ashmole, Esquire, and Mr William Lilly, Written by Themselves'' (T. Davies, London 1774), [https://books.google.com/books?id=DxE2AAAAMAAJ&pg=PA321 at p. 321] (Google).</ref>

===John Evelyn: Millenarianism===
Oughtred expressed [[Millenarianism|millenarian]] views to [[John Evelyn]] in 1655:<blockquote>"Came that renowned mathematician, Mr. Oughtred, to see me, I sending my coach to bring him to [[Wotton, Surrey|Wotton]], being now very aged. Among other discourse, he told me he thought water to be the [[Alchemy|philosopher]]'s [[Prima materia|first matter]], and that he was well persuaded of the possibility of their [[Philosopher's stone|elixir]]; he believed the sun to be a material fire, the moon a continent, as appears by the late [[Selenography|selenographers]]; he had strong apprehensions of some significant event to happen the following year, from the calculation of difference with the [[Genesis flood narrative|diluvian period]]; and added that it might possibly be to convert the Jews by our Saviour's [[Second Coming|visible appearance]], or to judge the world; and therefore, his word was, ''Parate in occursum'';<ref>I.e. "Praeparare in occursum Dei tui, Israel" (''[[Book of Amos]]'', Chapter IV, v. 12): "Prepare to meet thy God, O Israel".</ref> he said [[Original Sin]] was not met with in the [[Church Fathers#Greek Fathers|Greek Fathers]], yet he believed the thing; this was from some discourse on [[Jeremy Taylor|Dr. Taylor]]'s late book, which I had lent him."<ref>'Entry for 28 August 1655', in W. Bray (ed.), ''The Diary of John Evelyn'', with a Biographical introduction by the editor, and a special introduction by Richard Garnett, LL.D., 2 vols (M. Walter Dunne, New York and London 1901), I, [https://archive.org/details/diaryofjohnevely01eveliala/page/304 pp. 305-06] (Internet Archive, Retrieved 5 December 2018).</ref></blockquote>

==Oughtred Society==
Oughtred's name is remembered in the Oughtred Society, a group formed in the United States in 1991 for [[Collecting|collectors]] of slide rules. It produces the twice-yearly ''Journal of the Oughtred Society'' and holds meetings and auctions for its members.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Oughtred Society |url=http://www.oughtred.org/index.shtml |publisher=The Oughtred Society |access-date=18 March 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Brochure |url=http://www.oughtred.org/flyers/os-brochure-09.pdf |publisher=The Oughtred Society |access-date=18 March 2015}}</ref>
